2	import parsePath from "parse-path";
3	import normalizeUrl from "normalize-url";
4	
5	/**
6	 * parseUrl
7	 * Parses the input url.
8	 *
9	 * **Note**: This *throws* if invalid urls are provided.
10	 *
11	 * @name parseUrl
12	 * @function
13	 * @param {String} url The input url.
14	 * @param {Boolean|Object} normalize Whether to normalize the url or not.
15	 *                         Default is `false`. If `true`, the url will
16	 *                         be normalized. If an object, it will be the
17	 *                         options object sent to [`normalize-url`](https://github.com/sindresorhus/normalize-url).
18	 *
19	 *                         For SSH urls, normalize won't work.
20	 *
21	 * @return {Object} An object containing the following fields:
22	 *
23	 *    - `protocols` (Array): An array with the url protocols (usually it has one element).
24	 *    - `protocol` (String): The first protocol, `"ssh"` (if the url is a ssh url) or `"file"`.
25	 *    - `port` (null|Number): The domain port.
26	 *    - `resource` (String): The url domain (including subdomains).
27	 *    - `user` (String): The authentication user (usually for ssh urls).
28	 *    - `pathname` (String): The url pathname.
29	 *    - `hash` (String): The url hash.
30	 *    - `search` (String): The url querystring value.
31	 *    - `href` (String): The input url.
32	 *    - `query` (Object): The url querystring, parsed as object.
33	 *    - `parse_failed` (Boolean): Whether the parsing failed or not.
34	 */
35	const parseUrl = (url, normalize = false) => {
36	
37	    // Constants
38	    const GIT_RE = /(^(git@|http(s)?:\/\/)([\w\.\-@]+)(\/|:))(([\~,\.\w,\-,\_,\/]+)(.git){0,1}((\/){0,1}))/
39	
40	    const throwErr = msg => {
41	        const err = new Error(msg)
42	        err.subject_url = url
43	        throw err
44	    }
45	
46	    if (typeof url !== "string" || !url.trim()) {
47	        throwErr("Invalid url.")
48	    }
49	
50	    if (url.length > parseUrl.MAX_INPUT_LENGTH) {
51	        throwErr("Input exceeds maximum length. If needed, change the value of parseUrl.MAX_INPUT_LENGTH.")
52	    }
53	
54	    if (normalize) {
55	        if (typeof normalize !== "object") {
56	            normalize = {
57	                stripHash: false
58	            }
59	        }
60	        url = normalizeUrl(url, normalize)
61	    }
62	
63	    const parsed = parsePath(url)
64	
65	    // Potential git-ssh urls
66	    if (parsed.parse_failed) {
67	        const matched  = parsed.href.match(GIT_RE)
68	        if (matched) {
69	            parsed.protocols = ["ssh"]
70	            parsed.protocol = "ssh"
71	            parsed.resource = matched[4]
72	            parsed.host = matched[4]
73	            parsed.user = "git"
74	            parsed.pathname = `/${matched[6]}`
75	            parsed.parse_failed = false
76	        } else {
77	            throwErr("URL parsing failed.")
78	        }
79	    }
80	
81	    return parsed;
82	}
83	
84	parseUrl.MAX_INPUT_LENGTH = 2048
85	
86	export default parseUrl;
87

content.text:
All the first-party JS files are accounted for (src, dist build output, example, test). This is the `parse-url` npm package — a small URL/git-URL parser with no file I/O, no SQL, no shell/process execution, no templating, no XML processing, no deserialization, and no auth logic. I checked the only non-trivial piece of logic (the `GIT_RE` fallback regex in `src/index.js`) for a ReDoS/catastrophic-backtracking condition, since that's the sort of thing that bites regex-based parsers, but benchmarking it with inputs up to 32,000 characters showed linear, sub-millisecond behavior — no exploitable blowup.

None of the requested vulnerability classes (SQL/command/code/template injection, path traversal, SSRF, XSS, insecure deserialization, auth bypass, XXE) apply to this codebase's own code.
